explanations.answer: To fulfill His word spoken through Jeremiah the prophet
explanations.explanation: Ezra 1:1 says the LORD stirred Cyrus's spirit "…to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah…" The LORD had said it, and now He was making it happen. Cyrus, king of Persia, is the one who gets stirred, and then he puts a proclamation in writing for his whole kingdom. That's a king who doesn't lose the memo.

explanations.answer: To answer the prayers Cyrus himself had prayed
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd guess that, friend, but the text never mentions a prayer from Cyrus. It says the LORD stirred his spirit to fulfill the word spoken through Jeremiah, the prophet (Ezra 1:1). The reason on the page is God's own word, and I only bake with what's on the page. Cyrus, king of Persia, was just the one who got the stirring.

explanations.answer: To repay Judah for everything Babylon took
explanations.explanation: Nice thinking, but the verse doesn't say that. It gives one reason: the LORD stirred Cyrus's spirit "…to fulfill the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah…" (Ezra 1:1). Repaying isn't mentioned anywhere in it, friend, so nobody's handing out a refund receipt here.

Yes, a house. Cyrus says the LORD "…has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah." (Ezra 1:2). Cyrus, king of Persia, is the one saying it. A king with a whole kingdom to run, and he's announcing a house for the LORD, in writing, no less.

Wall is a good builder's guess, friend, but Cyrus doesn't say wall. He says the LORD "…has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah." (Ezra 1:2). The project on the table is a house for the LORD.

A throne sounds like a king thing to say, I'll give you that. But Cyrus says the LORD "…has appointed me to build a house for Him at Jerusalem in Judah." (Ezra 1:2). A house, not a throne. Cyrus isn't building anything for himself in this sentence.

Not quite, friend. Cyrus never brags about his armies. He says, "The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth…" (Ezra 1:2). In his own words, the kingdoms were given to him by the LORD.

Right, it's false. Cyrus says, "The LORD, the God of heaven, who has given me all the kingdoms of the earth…" (Ezra 1:2). He credits the LORD, not his armies. A king handing the credit to someone else, friend, I don't see that every day.

explanations.answer: That his God will be with him
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Cyrus says, "…may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah…" (Ezra 1:3). The wish is that God be with him. Cyrus is the king of Persia, and he's wishing it for people who belong to the LORD.

explanations.answer: That he will find his family's land
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since going home sounds like going to your land. But the wish in the verse is different: "…may his God be with him…" (Ezra 1:3). Family land isn't mentioned in that verse. Cyrus wishes them God's presence.

explanations.answer: That he will stay loyal to Persia
explanations.explanation: Ha, that's a king-sounding answer. But Cyrus wishes no such thing in the text. He says, "…may his God be with him, and may he go to Jerusalem in Judah…" (Ezra 1:3). His wish for them is that their God be with them.

Yes. Cyrus says, "…let every survivor, wherever he lives, be assisted by the men of that region with silver, gold, goods, and livestock…" (Ezra 1:4). That's a lot of help for one trip. A freewill offering for the house of God goes along with it too.

Careful there, friend. It's true. Cyrus says, "…let every survivor, wherever he lives, be assisted by the men of that region with silver, gold, goods, and livestock…" (Ezra 1:4). The proclamation puts the helping on the people around them.

True. Ezra 1:5 says the family heads of Judah and Benjamin, the priests and the Levites, "…everyone whose spirit God had stirred…" prepared to go. The same God who stirred the king also stirred them. I think that's a nice thing to notice.

It's actually true, friend. Ezra 1:5 names the family heads of Judah and Benjamin, with the priests and Levites, and calls them "…everyone whose spirit God had stirred…" What they share is that God stirred them. Same as He stirred Cyrus's spirit in verse 1.

explanations.answer: The articles from the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ezra 1:7 says Cyrus "…brought out the articles belonging to the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem…" Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon. They were headed back to where they belonged.

explanations.answer: The crown of Judah's last king
explanations.explanation: A crown would make a dramatic scene, friend, but it's not in the text. Ezra 1:7 says Cyrus brought out "…the articles belonging to the house of the LORD…" Those are what Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried away from Jerusalem.

Stones would be heavy, and I'd feel for whoever had to carry them. But the verse says something else. Cyrus brought out "…the articles belonging to the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem…" (Ezra 1:7). Nebuchadnezzar was the king of Babylon, and the articles are what he took.
True. Ezra 1:7 says Nebuchadnezzar had carried the articles away from Jerusalem and "…placed in the temple of his gods." Now King Cyrus is bringing them out. Good eye, baker.
It's true, friend. Ezra 1:7 says Nebuchadnezzar had carried the articles away from Jerusalem and "…placed in the temple of his gods." Then King Cyrus brought them out.

That's him. Ezra 1:8 says Mithredath the treasurer "…counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah." Verse 11 says Sheshbazzar brought all these along when the exiles went up from Babylon to Jerusalem. That's 5,400 articles, friend, and I'd want that man on inventory day.

Ezra's name is on the book, so I see why you went there. But he isn't who gets the articles in this passage. Mithredath the treasurer counted them out to "…Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah." (Ezra 1:8).

explanations.answer: Daniel the chief of the wise men
explanations.explanation: Daniel's a famous name, friend, and I see why it popped up. But Ezra 1:8 doesn't mention him. It says Mithredath the treasurer counted the articles out to "…Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah."

explanations.answer: They are kept out of the priesthood
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ezra 2:62 says these men searched for their family records, couldn't find them, and "…so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean." Records mattered for priests. I think this one hurts.

explanations.answer: They are sent back to Babylon
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text sends anyone back to Babylon. Ezra 2:62 says they searched for their family records, couldn't find them, and "…so were excluded from the priesthood as unclean." The consequence is about the priesthood, not where they live.

I can see the logic, since gatekeepers are on the list too. But the text doesn't give them that job. Ezra 2:62 says they "…were excluded from the priesthood as unclean." after they couldn't find their family records.

True. Ezra 2:63 says, "The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim." So the matter waits until there's a priest to consult them. Good eye, baker.

Careful, friend, this one is true. Ezra 2:63 says, "The governor ordered them not to eat the most holy things until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim." So it's a hold until a priest is there to consult them. I waited years in the back of a junk drawer, so I know how long "until" can feel.

explanations.answer: Some of the heads of the families
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ezra 2:68 says, "…some of the heads of the families gave freewill offerings to rebuild the house of God on its original site." Some of the heads of the families, that's who the verse names. You read that carefully, baker.

explanations.answer: Every family in the whole assembly
explanations.explanation: Every family is a big claim, friend. Ezra 2:68 says only that "…some of the heads of the families gave freewill offerings…" The verse says some, and I'll keep it at some.

explanations.answer: Only the priests and the Levites
explanations.explanation: The priests and Levites are in the passage, but not in this verse. Ezra 2:68 says "…some of the heads of the families gave freewill offerings…" when they arrived at the house of the LORD. That's the group named.
Not this time, friend. Ezra 2:68 says they gave "…to rebuild the house of God on its original site." Original, not brand-new. The house goes back where it stood.

Right, it's False. Ezra 2:68 says they gave "…to rebuild the house of God on its original site." So the plan was to put it back where it stood, not to start over somewhere new. I know that feeling. When I got pulled out of that drawer, nobody asked me to find a new kitchen. They just wanted me back on the counter.

explanations.answer: As much as each is able
explanations.explanation: That's it. Ezra 2:69 says, "According to their ability, they gave to the treasury for this work…" Each gave what he could. The verse lists 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver and 100 priestly garments.

Same amount is a fair thought, friend. Ezra 2:69 says, "According to their ability, they gave to the treasury for this work…" The measure the verse gives is ability, and no set amount per person is named.

explanations.answer: A tenth of what each owns
explanations.explanation: A tenth sounds tidy, friend, but no fraction shows up in the verse. Ezra 2:69 says, "According to their ability, they gave to the treasury for this work…" Each gave by his ability.
